steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on detecting spinal osteophytes in X-rays with a segmentation-based patch extraction method. Explain why osteophytes matter, what has been done before on osteophyte detection, and what our contributions are.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

1. Osteophytes and why they matter
2. Imaging and automated detection of spinal osteophytes
3. Osteophyte detection in other parts of the body
4. Motivation: no automated method for spinal X-rays
5. Our contributions: SegPatch and evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

1. Osteophytes
- feature of osteoarthritis (OA): fibrocartilage-capped bony outgrowths
- strong role in severity and progression of OA
- impinge nerves, e.g. spinal roots; issues in many other spinal diseases

2. Spinal osteophytes
- manual identification generally via MRI
- X-rays limited: quality, 2D nature of conventional radiography
- Wang et al.: region proposals, classified from unwrapped cortical shell maps, Positron Emission Tomography and Computed Tomography scans of thoracic and lumbar vertebral bodies; 85% sensitivity at 2 false positives per patient

3. Other body parts
- Ebsim et al.: hip osteophytes in dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, segmentation with U-Net + manual cropping
- Banerjee et al: hand osteophytes in X-rays, cellular neural networks (communication only between neighboring units); automated ground truth but no clinical representative
- VinDr-SpineXR: extensive dataset, baselines for multiple spinal diseases incl. osteophytes; poor results, performance increases with label size; matches our detection findings (sec 5.3)

4. Motivation
- number and size of osteophytes ~ estimate of OA progress
- expert annotation time-consuming, expensive, error-prone (inter-/intra-reader variability), esp. tiny structures
- no automated method for spinal osteophyte detection on spinal X-rays (to our knowledge)

5. Contributions
- method to automatically identify osteophytes from conventional spinal radiography
- SegPatch: patches from deep-learning based vertebrae body segmentation
- unlike tiling: patches tied to potential osteophyte locations
- multiple neural network classifiers; evaluated on public NHANESII; compared to tiling baseline -> significant advantage

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Osteophytes are one of the features seen in osteoarthritis (OA). They are bony outgrowths capped with fibrocartilage. They play a strong role in determining how severe OA is and how it progresses. Osteophytes also cause problems because they impinge nerves, such as spinal roots, and they are a significant issue in many other spinal diseases too.

Osteophytes have generally been identified manually using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). X-rays on the other hand have been used less, because of the challenges coming from the quality and the 2D nature of conventional radiography. There has also been work on detecting spinal osteophytes automatically. Wang et al. extracted region proposals and classified them from unwrapped cortical shell maps in Positron Emission Tomography and Computed Tomography scans of the vertebral bodies of the thoracic and lumbar spine. They got 85% sensitivity at 2 false positive detections per patient.

Automated approaches for detecting osteophytes in other parts of the body have also been proposed. Ebsim et al. identified hip osteophytes in dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry by segmenting the osteophyte regions with U-Net and manual cropping (to highlight the area of interest). Banerjee et al identified hand osteophytes in X-rays using cellular neural networks (neural networks where communication is only allowed between neighboring units). They automated the ground truth acquisition, but no actual clinical representative was involved at any point in the acquisition process. The VinDr-SpineXR study gives an extensive dataset with baseline results on multiple spinal diseases, osteophytes included. Their results are poor (and performance goes up as label size goes up), which matches what we found for detection in sec 5.3.

- number and size of osteophytes ~ estimate of OA progress
- expert annotations time-consuming, expensive, prone to errors (inter- and intra-reader variability), esp. tiny structures like osteophytes
- to our knowledge no automated method for spinal osteophyte detection on spinal X-rays

Contributions:
- method to automatically identify osteophytes from conventional spinal radiography
- SegPatch: robust patch extraction via deep-learning based vertebrae body segmentation
- unlike standard tiling, patches associated with potential osteophyte locations
- trained multiple neural network classifiers; evaluated on public NHANESII; compared with tiling baseline -> significant advantage of SegPatch

steps.text:
## Introduction

Osteophytes are one of the features seen in osteoarthritis (OA). They are bony outgrowths capped with fibrocartilage. They play a strong role in determining how severe OA is and how it progresses. Osteophytes also cause problems because they impinge nerves, such as spinal roots, and they are a significant issue in many other spinal diseases too.

Osteophytes have generally been identified manually using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). X-rays on the other hand have been used less, because of the challenges coming from the quality and the 2D nature of conventional radiography. There has also been work on detecting spinal osteophytes automatically. Wang et al. extracted region proposals and classified them from unwrapped cortical shell maps in Positron Emission Tomography and Computed Tomography scans of the vertebral bodies of the thoracic and lumbar spine. They got 85% sensitivity at 2 false positive detections per patient.

Automated approaches for detecting osteophytes in other parts of the body have also been proposed. Ebsim et al. identified hip osteophytes in dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry by segmenting the osteophyte regions with U-Net and manual cropping (to highlight the area of interest). Banerjee et al identified hand osteophytes in X-rays using cellular neural networks (neural networks where communication is only allowed between neighboring units). They automated the ground truth acquisition, but no actual clinical representative was involved at any point in the acquisition process. The VinDr-SpineXR study gives an extensive dataset with baseline results on multiple spinal diseases, osteophytes included. Their results are poor (and performance goes up as label size goes up), which matches what we found for detection in sec 5.3.

The number and the size of the osteophytes could be seen as an estimate of how far OA has progressed. Annotations by clinical experts take a lot of time and are expensive, and they are also prone to errors (i.e. inter- and intra-reader variability). This is especially true for tiny structures like osteophytes. As far as we know, there is no automated method for detecting spinal osteophytes on spinal X-rays.

Our contributions are as follows. We developed a method that automatically identifies osteophytes from conventional spinal radiography. First, we proposed SegPatch, a robust mechanism that extracts patches from the spinal X-ray images using a deep-learning based vertebrae body segmentation approach. Different from the standard tiling approach, the new patching gives patches that are associated with places where osteophytes could potentially be. After that, we trained multiple neural network models for classification. We evaluated our framework on NHANESII, a publicly available spine X-ray data set, and compared SegPatch with the baseline tiling method. The results show that using SegPatch has a significant advantage.

steps.text:
## Introduction

One of the features observed in osteoarthritis (OA) [1] are osteophytes, which are fibrocartilage-capped bony outgrowths. They play a strong role in determining the severity and progression of OA. Osteophytes also cause problems by impinging nerves such as spinal roots [2], and pose significant issues in many other spinal diseases.

The manual identification of osteophytes has generally been done using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) [3]. In contrast, the use of X-rays has been limited due to the challenges associated with the quality and 2D nature of conventional radiography. Automated detection of spinal osteophytes has also been explored. Wang et al. [4] extracted region proposals and classified them from unwrapped cortical shell maps in Positron Emission Tomography and Computed Tomography scans of the vertebral bodies of the thoracic and lumbar spine, achieving 85% sensitivity at 2 false positive detections per patient.

Automated approaches to detect osteophytes in other parts of the body have been proposed as well. Ebsim et al., [5] identified hip osteophytes in dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry by segmenting the osteophyte regions using U-Net [6] and manual cropping (to highlight the area of interest). Banerjee et al [7] identified hand osteophytes in X-rays through cellular neural networks (neural networks where communication is allowed only between neighboring units). They automated the ground truth acquisition, but without any involvement from an actual clinical representative throughout the acquisition process. The VinDr-SpineXR study [8] provides an extensive dataset with baseline results on multiple spinal diseases, including osteophytes. Its poor results (and the trend of increasing performance with increasing label size) match our detection findings in sec 5.3.

The number and size of the osteophytes could be seen as an estimate of OA progress. Clinical experts' annotations are time-consuming and expensive, and prone to errors (i.e. inter- and intra-reader variability), especially for tiny structures such as osteophytes. To the best of our knowledge, there has been no automated method for spinal osteophyte detection for spinal X-rays.

Our contributions are as follows - We have developed a method to automatically identify osteophytes from conventional spinal radiography. First, we proposed a robust mechanism, SegPatch, to extract patches from the spinal X-ray images through a deep-learning based vertebrae body segmentation approach [9].

Unlike the standard tiling approach, the proposed patching generates patches that are associated with potential locations of the osteophytes. We then trained multiple neural network models for classification. Our framework was evaluated on the publicly available spine X-ray data set NHANESII, and SegPatch was compared with the baseline tiling method. The results show a significant advantage of using SegPatch.

References:
[1] Peter M Van Der Kraan and Wim B Van Den Berg, “Osteophytes: relevance and biology,” Osteoarthritis and cartilage , vol. 15, no. 3, pp. 237–244, 2007.
